questions.question: A loss X is measured in euros. Its premium is $\Pi(X)=\mathbb{E}[X]+\alpha\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}$, with dimensionless $\alpha>0$. Why is the square root needed for the loading term?
options: It converts euro variance into a dimensionless probability.
It makes the mean and loading both squared-euro quantities.
It converts squared-euro variance into a euro amount.
It turns every loading into a fixed percentage of the mean.

questions.question: A non-negative loss X has finite mean but $\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\infty$. An insurer proposes a finite SD premium with fixed coefficient $\alpha>0$. Does finite mean alone justify the proposed finite price?
options: Yes; the square root makes every infinite variance finite.
No; this rule requires a finite second moment for a finite SD loading.
Yes; finite mean implies a finite standard deviation for non-negative losses.
Yes; capping the loss at a finite maximum gives the original loss a finite SD price.

questions.question: For a non-negative loss X with finite second moment, $\Pi(X)=\mathbb{E}[X]+\alpha\sigma_X$ with fixed $\alpha>0$. If the premium equals the mean exactly, what follows about the loss law?
options: X must have mean zero rather than a positive certain amount.
X can remain random whenever its support is bounded.
The loading coefficient alpha must be zero.
X is constant almost surely.

questions.question: A nonconstant non-negative insured loss X is proposed as a test of the SD premium’s proportionality by comparing $\Pi(-X)$ with $-\Pi(X)$. Why is this not a valid test of its stated positive-scale property?
options: The negative scaling lies outside the stated insured-loss and scaling domain.
Loss scaling must keep standard deviation unchanged.
A fixed loading coefficient forbids every monetary rescaling.
The property requires independent copies instead of a scaled loss.

questions.question: A loss has mean $\mu>0$, spread $\sigma\ge0$ and SD premium $\Pi=\mu+\alpha\sigma$, with fixed coefficient $\alpha>0$. Which formula for its loading as a fraction of expected loss is valid for every admissible loss and coefficient?
options: $\alpha$.
$\alpha\sigma/\mu$.
$\alpha\mu/\sigma$.
$\sigma/\alpha$.

questions.question: A loss has mean ten and variance nine. Under $\Pi(X)=\mathbb{E}[X]+\alpha\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}$ with $\alpha=1/2$, what is its premium?
A non-negative loss X has SD premium twelve at a fixed loading coefficient. A certain charge of seven is added to every loss outcome. What is the SD premium of X+7?
A non-negative loss X has SD premium twelve. The loss amount is rescaled to 3X using the same fixed dimensionless coefficient. What price does positive proportionality give?
A loss has mean eight and standard deviation three. A quoted price fourteen is to equal its SD premium $\Pi=8+\alpha(3)$. What positive loading coefficient does this quote imply?
Independent losses X,Y have means ten and twenty and standard deviations three and four. With fixed $\alpha=1$, what is their pooled SD premium $\Pi(X+Y)$?

For independent losses with finite spreads $\sigma_X,\sigma_Y\ge0$ and fixed $\alpha>0$, pooled loading is $\alpha\sqrt{\sigma_X^2+\sigma_Y^2}$. What necessary and sufficient spread condition makes it equal the sum of separate SD loadings exactly?
options: Whenever the two positive spreads are equal.
Whenever the two loss means are equal.
When at least one of the two spreads is zero.
Only when the loading coefficient is greater than one.

questions.question: Losses $X,Y$ have equal means and finite second moments, with $\operatorname{Var}(X)\le\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. Both use $\Pi(Z)=\mathbb{E}[Z]+\alpha\sigma_Z$, where $\sigma_Z$ is standard deviation and the same $\alpha>0$ is used. Why is $\Pi(X)\le\Pi(Y)$?
options: The common mean cancels, and square roots preserve the variance comparison.
Equal means remove the loading, so both premiums equal the common mean.
The larger variance requires a higher coefficient for Y in this definition.
A common positive coefficient reverses the direction of the variance order.

questions.question: A bounded nonconstant loss has mean $\mu$, positive standard deviation $\sigma$, and essential maximum b. No rip-off for its SD price requires $\mu+\alpha\sigma\le b$. Which restriction is equivalent for every such loss law?
options: $\alpha\le(b-\mu)/\sigma$.
$\alpha\ge(b-\mu)/\sigma$.
$\alpha\le(b+\mu)/\sigma$.
$\alpha\le(b-\mu)/\sigma^2$.

questions.question: Four independent identical losses each have mean ten and standard deviation two. At $\alpha=1$, what is the pooled total SD premium divided by four, expressed as price per policy?

Two losses have mean and standard deviation $(5,4)$ and $(7,1)$. Under the common rule $\Pi=\mu+\alpha\sigma$, for exactly which range of positive coefficients is the first loss more expensive than the second?
options: $\alpha>2$.

questions.question: A loss X is one or five with equal probability. Two policies are coupled as identical copies, so their combined loss is 2X. At $\alpha=1$, compare $\Pi(2X)$ with $2\Pi(X)$.
options: They are $6+\sqrt{8}$ and $10$.
They are $22$ and $10$.
Both equal $10$.
They are $10$ and $6$.

questions.question: Let X be zero or two with equal probability and Y certainly two, coupled so $X\le Y$ in every outcome. Both prices use SD coefficient $\alpha=2$. Does this pointwise increased loss necessarily receive a higher SD price?
options: Yes; X costs one while Y costs two, so the price follows the loss order.
Yes; X costs three while Y costs four because both have the same spread.
No; the comparison is inadmissible because X may be zero.
No; X costs three while Y costs two because Y loses the spread loading.

questions.question: Loss X is zero or two with equal probability. Loss Y takes 0,1,3 with probabilities 1/3,1/2,1/6. Both have mean one and variance one. They receive the same SD premium for every $\alpha>0$. Does agreement across all coefficients identify their laws?
options: No; their zero-loss probabilities differ despite matching price-relevant moments.
Yes; every coefficient gives a separate probability equation identifying each mass.
Yes; equal variance and mean force equal loss distributions.
No; the premiums actually differ because Y has three possible outcomes.

questions.question: At $\alpha=1$, a class C has two equally likely values. Conditional on its first value, loss X is 3 or 5 equally likely; conditional on its second, X is 1 or 7 equally likely. Apply the same SD rule conditionally and then to that random conditional premium. What comparison tests iterativity?
options: $\Pi(X)=\Pi(\Pi(X\mid C))=6$.
$\Pi(X)=\Pi(\Pi(X\mid C))=4+\sqrt{5}$.
$\Pi(X)=4+\sqrt{5}$ while $\Pi(\Pi(X\mid C))=7$.
$\Pi(X)=4+\sqrt{5}$ while $\Pi(\Pi(X\mid C))=6$.

questions.question: Fix any SD coefficient $\alpha>0$. Choose a unit Bernoulli loss with probability $p=1/(1+\alpha^2/4)$ of loss one. Then $\sqrt{(1-p)/p}=\alpha/2$. Does this family allow one fixed positive coefficient to ensure no rip-off for every bounded loss?
options: Yes; a sufficiently small fixed alpha works for every such probability.
No; its premium exceeds one for the chosen law, however small alpha is.
Yes; the Bernoulli variance bound guarantees every SD premium is below one.
No; the chosen p is outside the probability interval for positive alpha.
